strengths: Addresses important practical phenomenon with surprising empirical findings: weak diffusion priors can match strong-prior performance, challenging conventional wisdom
Exceptionally comprehensive experimental validation spanning multiple inverse problems, datasets, baselines, and prior strengths with systematic ablation studies
Rigorous theoretical analysis providing multiple complementary explanations: posterior consistency (Theorem 3.1), data dominance in high-dimensional settings (Theorem 3.2), and shared local structure
Honest treatment of limitations with clear identification of failure cases (box inpainting, large super-resolution), showing theory is incomplete
Strong reproducibility with detailed hyperparameter specifications, clear experimental configurations, and promised code release
Practical algorithmic contributions (ADAMSPHERE, HOLDOUTTOPK) that improve reconstruction with weak priors
Well-designed visualizations effectively demonstrating reconstruction quality progression and spatial autocorrelation diagnostics
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Theorem 3.1 largely formalizes standard Bayesian consistency (Schwartz 1965), and Theorem 3.2 presents intuitive result that informative measurements dominate priors
Theory-practice gap: Assumptions in Theorem 3.2 (especially δ₀-identifiability) are difficult to verify for real problems; no clear procedure for practitioners to check applicability
Incomplete failure-mode prediction: spatial autocorrelation diagnostic shows uniformly high correlations (0.95+) across all settings, providing limited discriminative power for predicting failures

Missing cost-benefit quantification: paper lacks explicit computational savings analysis, wallclock time comparisons, or memory usage across prior strengths, making practical value proposition unclear
Unquantified practical advantages: unclear when quality loss from weak priors becomes acceptable relative to computational savings, limiting actionability for practitioners
Limited practical guidance: no clear decision rules for when to use weak priors (e.g., measurement informativeness thresholds) or how to predict failure a priori
Sparse ablation studies: insufficient sensitivity analysis on early-stopping strategy, measurement noise levels, and systematic variation of measurement dimensionality
Presentation issues: important results relegated to appendices (e.g., cross-domain results), and connection between three explanatory mechanisms could be clearer
